Massachusetts.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back only through a pardon from the governor.
Massachusetts.process_note: You apply to the Massachusetts Parole Board, which reviews the case and recommends for or against a pardon to the governor, who decides with the Governor's Council.
Massachusetts.waiting_period: 10 years after sentencing or release from incarceration for a felony pardon
Massachusetts.agency_name: Massachusetts Parole Board (Advisory Board of Pardons)
Massachusetts.state_note: Sealing a record does not restore firearm rights, and only certain low-level misdemeanors can go to the Firearms Licensing Review Board instead.

Michigan.restoration_note: Firearm rights come back automatically for most felonies, and by court petition for more serious felonies.
Michigan.process_note: For most felonies rights return on their own 3 years after the sentence, fines, and probation or parole are done; for a specified felony you must wait 5 years and ask the circuit court to restore them.
Michigan.waiting_period: 3 years after the sentence ends for most felonies; 5 years for a specified felony
Michigan.statute_name: Restoration of rights to possess a firearm
Michigan.state_note: A specified felony means one involving force, drugs, a firearm, explosives, or burglary or arson of an occupied home, and those cases always need a judge's order.

Minnesota.restoration_note: A person convicted of a crime of violence can ask a judge to restore the right to possess firearms.
Minnesota.process_note: You file a petition in the court in the county where you were convicted, show good cause, and show you have been released from confinement.
Minnesota.waiting_period: no fixed period to file a first petition; 3 years to refile if a petition is denied
Minnesota.statute_name: Restoration of civil rights; possession of firearms
Minnesota.state_note: A person convicted of a crime of violence is banned from possessing a firearm for life unless a judge restores the right under this law.

Mississippi.restoration_note: A person with a felony conviction can get firearm rights back through a pardon, a court certificate of rehabilitation, or expungement of an eligible felony.
Mississippi.process_note: You can ask the court that convicted you for a certificate of rehabilitation by showing you have lived a law-abiding, productive life since the sentence ended, or you can seek a pardon from the governor.
Mississippi.waiting_period: 7 years after the sentence ends to apply for a pardon; no fixed period for a court certificate of rehabilitation
Mississippi.statute_name: Unlawful possession of a firearm by a convicted felon; certificate of rehabilitation
Mississippi.agency_name: Office of the Governor of Mississippi
Mississippi.state_note: A pardon restores gun rights, but the governor's office has an informal rule of waiting 7 years after the sentence is complete before applying.

Missouri.restoration_note: Firearm rights can come back by expunging an eligible felony, but serious and violent felonies can never be expunged.
Missouri.process_note: You file a petition in the court that convicted you asking to expunge the felony, and if the court grants it, your firearm rights are restored.
Missouri.waiting_period: 3 years after completing the sentence, probation, or parole for a felony expungement
Missouri.state_note: Class A felonies and dangerous felonies, including murder, robbery, and kidnapping, can never be expunged in Missouri.

Montana.restoration_note: Most people with a felony conviction get their rights back automatically when state supervision ends, and only a small group faces a state firearm ban.
Montana.process_note: Rights return on their own when the sentence and supervision end; if the felony drew a weapon sentence or requires sex or violent offender registration, you must ask the district court for a permit to possess a firearm.
Montana.waiting_period: none — rights return when state supervision ends for most felonies
Montana.agency_name: Montana Board of Pardons and Parole
Montana.state_note: Montana's state firearm ban is narrow and covers only felonies with a weapon sentence or ones that require sex or violent offender registration.

Nebraska.restoration_note: Firearm rights can come back only through a pardon that expressly gives the governor's permission to possess a firearm.
Nebraska.process_note: You apply to the Nebraska Board of Pardons, and if the Board grants a pardon it must separately empower the governor to expressly authorize you to receive, possess, or transport a firearm.
Nebraska.waiting_period: 10 years after the sentence ends with a clean record for a felony pardon
Nebraska.state_note: A pardon alone does not restore gun rights in Nebraska — the Board must expressly authorize firearm possession as a separate step.

Nevada.restoration_note: Only a full, unconditional pardon from the Board of Pardons Commissioners restores firearm rights in Nevada.
Nevada.process_note: You apply to the Board of Pardons Commissioners, and if granted a full, unconditional pardon you are restored to all civil rights, including the right to bear arms.
Nevada.waiting_period: no fixed period — the Board looks for good conduct over a substantial period of time
Nevada.state_note: Sealing a criminal record in Nevada does not restore the right to bear arms — only a pardon does.

New Hampshire.restoration_note: A single nonviolent felony can be annulled by the sentencing court, which restores firearm rights, but violent crimes and multiple felonies cannot be annulled.
New Hampshire.process_note: You file a petition for annulment in the court that sentenced you, and the judge grants it if annulment will help your rehabilitation and is consistent with public welfare.
New Hampshire.waiting_period: 5 years after the sentence ends for a Class B felony; 10 years for a Class A felony
New Hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire only bans firearm possession for felonies against a person or property or felony drug offenses, and annulment is not available for violent crimes or extended-term sentences.

New Jersey.restoration_note: Firearm rights can come back by expunging an eligible conviction, but many serious crimes can never be expunged.
New Jersey.process_note: You apply to the Superior Court for an expungement, and once granted the conviction is deemed not to have occurred.
New Jersey.waiting_period: 5 years after the sentence ends for an indictable offense (4 years in compelling circumstances); 10 years for a clean slate expungement
New Jersey.state_note: Criminal homicide, robbery, arson, sexual assault, kidnapping, and most drug distribution offenses can never be expunged in New Jersey.
